Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- It arrived in Rich Stevens' mailbox a few weeks ago: the notice that Citibank had "rate-jacked" the Visa cards belonging to him and his wife. Some credit card holders have seen their interest rates go up dramatically, a practice called "rate-jacking." "In my case, from 9.5 percent to 16.99," the 54-year-old nurse from the Long Island hamlet of Merrick, New York, told CNN. And his wife's rate zoomed from 7.95 percent to 16.99 percent, he said. Stevens said he did not know why the rates had soared; his credit rating is great. But, like thousands of other credit card customers around the nation, he has been notified his rate is skyrocketing. "It almost borders on loan-sharking, from my perspective," he said. In the blogosphere, writers are livid at the instant rate hikes -- called "rate-jacking." Citigroup seems to be the target of most bloggers' venom -- partly because Citigroup issues so many credit cards and partly because Citi began sending the notices at about the same time it was getting a $20 billion, taxpayer-financed government bailout. No one at Citigroup would talk on camera to CNN about the matter. Instead, the company issued a written statement, which said: "To continue funding in this difficult credit and funding environment, Citi is repricing a group of customers." Citi told CNN that anyone unhappy with the new rates can opt out and continue paying the lower interest, but they must close their account when their card expires. It's all in the fine print. Rep. Carolyn Maloney, D-New York, said she is sick of the fine print. She agreed that credit card companies get away with whatever they want, as long at they put their desires into the fine print. "They have this provision that says they can raise the rate -- any time, any reason," she said. In September, Maloney got the House to pass by an overwhelming margin of 200 votes the "credit card holders' bill of rights," which would have stopped rate-jacking and the imposition of other fees by banks. But the bill has languished in the Senate since September. "There's a lot of pushback from the financial industry," she said.  Watch how card companies are trying to woo customers » . Critics say that pushback is linked to donations from the banking industry to the politicians responsible for regulating credit cards. The chairman of the Senate Banking Committee is Christopher Dodd. His staff said the Connecticut Democrat has his own credit card bill containing tough language to stop things like rate-jacking and shortening of billing cycles -- two issues that anger consumers. But even Dodd's own bill has failed to gain traction -- it has sat since July. Dodd himself received more than $4 million from the financial sector during the last campaign, according to campaign records. His office did not respond to CNN's questions about that. It did say that he has tried repeatedly to protect consumers, but added, "legislation has been met with stiff opposition by the credit card industry." On Thursday, the Federal Reserve is expected to vote on its own new rules regarding credit cards, rules in the works for four years that could clamp down on rate-jacking. Whatever is passed, Maloney said, probably would not take effect until 2010.

(CNN) — A notice arrived in Rich Stevens’ mailbox a few weeks ago informing him that Citibank had “rate-jacked” the Visa cards held by him and his wife.

Some credit card holders have seen their interest rates rise dramatically—a practice known as “rate-jacking.”

“In my case, from 9.5 percent to 16.99,” the 54-year-old nurse from the Long Island hamlet of Merrick, New York, told CNN. His wife’s rate surged from 7.95 percent to 16.99 percent, he said.

Stevens said he did not know why the rates had soared, particularly because his credit rating is excellent. But, like thousands of other credit card customers across the country, he has been notified that his rate is skyrocketing.

“It almost borders on loan-sharking, from my perspective,” he said.

Across the blogosphere, writers are livid about the sudden rate increases. Citigroup appears to be the primary target of bloggers’ anger—partly because it issues so many credit cards and partly because Citi began sending the notices at about the same time it was receiving a $20 billion, taxpayer-financed government bailout.

No one at Citigroup would speak with CNN on camera about the matter. Instead, the company issued a written statement: “To continue funding in this difficult credit and funding environment, Citi is repricing a group of customers.”

Citi told CNN that customers unhappy with the new rates may opt out and continue paying the lower interest rate, but they must close their accounts when their cards expire. It is all in the fine print.

Rep. Carolyn Maloney, D-New York, said she is tired of the fine print. She agreed that credit card companies can get away with whatever they want, provided they include their terms in the fine print.

“They have this provision that says they can raise the rate—any time, any reason,” she said.

In September, Maloney persuaded the House to pass the “Credit Cardholders’ Bill of Rights” by an overwhelming margin of 200 votes. The measure would have stopped rate-jacking and banks’ imposition of other fees. However, the bill has languished in the Senate since September.

“There’s a lot of pushback from the financial industry,” she said.

Watch how card companies are trying to woo customers ».

Critics say that opposition is linked to banking-industry donations to the politicians responsible for regulating credit cards.

The chairman of the Senate Banking Committee is Christopher Dodd. His staff said the Connecticut Democrat has introduced his own credit card bill, which includes tough provisions designed to stop practices such as rate-jacking and shortening billing cycles—two issues that anger consumers.

But even Dodd’s bill has failed to gain traction; it has remained stalled since July.

According to campaign records, Dodd received more than $4 million from the financial sector during the last campaign. His office did not respond to CNN’s questions about those contributions. It did say that he has repeatedly sought to protect consumers, but added that “legislation has been met with stiff opposition by the credit card industry.”

On Thursday, the Federal Reserve is expected to vote on its own new credit card rules. Four years in the making, the rules could clamp down on rate-jacking.

Whatever is approved, Maloney said, probably would not take effect until 2010.
outputs.L2:
A few weeks earlier, Rich Stevens received a letter informing him that Citibank had sharply increased the interest rates on the Visa cards held by him and his wife—a practice commonly known as “rate-jacking.”

Stevens, a 54-year-old nurse from Merrick, a hamlet on Long Island, New York, told CNN that his rate had risen from 9.5 percent to 16.99 percent. His wife’s rate jumped from 7.95 percent to 16.99 percent.

He said he could not understand the reason for the increases because he had an excellent credit rating. Nevertheless, he joined thousands of credit card customers nationwide who had been notified of steep rate hikes.

“From my perspective, it comes close to loan-sharking,” Stevens said.

Online commentators have reacted furiously to these sudden increases. Citigroup has drawn much of their anger, partly because it is a major credit card issuer and partly because it began mailing the notices around the same time it received a $20 billion government bailout funded by taxpayers.

Citigroup declined CNN’s request for an on-camera interview. The company instead released a written statement saying that, to maintain funding amid difficult credit and financing conditions, Citi was changing the pricing for a group of customers.

The company also told CNN that customers who objected to the higher rates could reject them and keep paying the lower interest rate. However, they would have to close their accounts once their cards expired—a condition disclosed in the fine print.

Rep. Carolyn Maloney, a New York Democrat, said she was tired of such fine-print provisions. In her view, credit card companies can do almost anything they choose as long as the terms are buried in the contract. She pointed to language allowing issuers to raise rates at any time and for any reason.

In September, Maloney persuaded the House to approve the “Credit Cardholders’ Bill of Rights” by an overwhelming 200-vote margin. The measure would have prohibited rate-jacking and other bank-imposed fees. Since then, however, it has remained stalled in the Senate. Maloney attributed the delay to strong resistance from the financial industry.

At the same time, card companies were attempting to attract customers.

Critics argue that the industry’s opposition is connected to banking-sector campaign contributions made to lawmakers who oversee credit card regulation.

Sen. Christopher Dodd, the Connecticut Democrat who chaired the Senate Banking Committee, had introduced his own credit card legislation. According to his staff, the proposal included strong provisions aimed at preventing practices such as rate-jacking and shortened billing cycles, both of which had angered consumers.

Dodd’s bill also failed to advance and had been sitting idle since July. Campaign records showed that he received more than $4 million from the financial sector during the previous election campaign. His office did not answer CNN’s questions about those contributions. It did, however, say that Dodd had repeatedly sought to protect consumers, while noting that his legislative efforts had encountered intense opposition from the credit card industry.

The Federal Reserve was expected to vote Thursday on separate credit card regulations that had been under development for four years and could restrict rate-jacking. Maloney said that whatever rules were approved would probably not become effective until 2010.

Citibank sharply increased interest rates for some credit card customers, including Rich Stevens and his wife, even though they had maintained a strong credit history. The move surprised many customers who believed their responsible borrowing and payment records would protect them from steep rate increases.

The practice, commonly known as “rate-jacking,” has angered thousands of cardholders and prompted widespread criticism online. Customers have complained that banks can impose significantly higher rates even when an individual has consistently paid bills on time and has not shown signs of increased credit risk.

Citigroup said it was repricing certain accounts to maintain funding in a difficult credit environment. The company noted that affected customers could reject the new rates and continue paying their existing balances at the lower rate. However, those who opt out must stop using the card and close the account when it expires.

The controversy has also increased pressure for legislative reform. Rep. Supporters argued that such protections would make credit card terms fairer and more predictable for consumers.
outputs.L4:
Credit card companies have angered consumers by sharply increasing interest rates even for customers who have consistently paid their bills on time and maintained good credit. The practice, often called “rate-jacking,” can leave cardholders paying far more to carry the same balance, sometimes with little warning and without any obvious change in their financial circumstances.

Citigroup became a prominent target of criticism after customers reported receiving notices that their annual percentage rates would rise dramatically, in some cases nearly doubling. Many cardholders said they had chosen Citi because of its comparatively low rates and had upheld their end of the agreement by making timely payments. They therefore viewed the increases as arbitrary and unfair, particularly when closing the account or transferring the balance could create additional costs or harm their credit.

Citi defended the changes by pointing to broader economic conditions and the rising cost and risk of lending. The company said it periodically reviewed customer accounts and adjusted pricing in response to market conditions, credit risk, and the need to manage its overall card portfolio. It also maintained that customers were notified and, in some cases, could reject the new terms—although doing so could mean losing access to the card and paying off the existing balance under specified conditions.

Those explanations did little to ease public frustration. Consumers and advocates argued that credit card agreements gave issuers too much power to alter interest rates and fees after customers had already accumulated debt. A rate that appeared manageable when purchases were made could suddenly become much more expensive, increasing minimum payments and making balances harder to eliminate.

The controversy drew attention in Congress, where lawmakers questioned credit card executives about pricing practices, disclosures, penalty fees, and retroactive rate increases. Critics said the industry’s complex contracts and broad discretion placed consumers at a severe disadvantage. They called for rules that would make rates more predictable and prevent companies from changing the cost of existing debt without a clear justification.

Mounting outrage over rate-jacking helped build support for a credit cardholders’ bill of rights in the House of Representatives. The legislation sought to restrict arbitrary interest-rate increases, curb certain fees, require clearer notice of changes, and give consumers more time and information to respond. Supporters described the measure as a necessary correction to abusive industry practices, while card issuers warned that tighter restrictions could reduce access to credit or raise costs for other borrowers.

For affected customers, however, the issue was straightforward: they had paid on time, preserved good credit, and still saw their rates soar. Their experiences helped turn an obscure feature of credit card contracts into a national political issue and intensified demands for stronger consumer protections.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Citibank sharply increasing customers’ credit card interest rates during the financial crisis, including consumer reactions and proposed congressional action.
counterfactuals.output:
# Citibank credit card rate hikes draw consumer anger, congressional scrutiny

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Citibank customers are expressing outrage after the bank sharply increased interest rates on some credit card accounts during the financial crisis, in some cases pushing annual percentage rates toward 30%.

The increases arrived as many Americans were already struggling with layoffs, declining home values and tighter access to credit. Several cardholders said they had paid their bills on time and were surprised to receive notices imposing substantially higher rates.

“I did everything I was supposed to do, and suddenly carrying a balance became much more expensive,” one customer said. “It feels like the rules changed in the middle of the game.”

Citibank, part of Citigroup, said it periodically adjusts account terms based on market conditions, borrowing costs and customers’ risk profiles. Customers receiving new terms generally could reject them and close or stop using the account, though they would still have to repay any outstanding balance under the applicable terms.

Consumer advocates said that option offered little relief to households that depended on credit cards for basic expenses. Closing an account can also reduce available credit and potentially affect a borrower’s credit score.

The increases drew additional criticism because Citigroup received billions of dollars in federal support as the government sought to stabilize the banking system. Critics argued that taxpayers were helping rescue financial institutions while some of those same banks were making credit more expensive for consumers.

Members of Congress responded by calling for faster and stronger limits on credit card practices. Proposed measures included restricting rate increases on existing balances, requiring clearer notice of changes and preventing banks from raising rates unless a customer was significantly delinquent or had agreed to a variable-rate arrangement.

Lawmakers also discussed freezing certain rate increases until new consumer protections could take effect. Supporters said immediate action was necessary to prevent issuers from repricing accounts before tougher rules became law.

Banking industry representatives warned that strict limits could cause lenders to reduce credit lines, impose new fees or stop extending credit to higher-risk borrowers. They said rising defaults during the recession required banks to account for greater losses.

For cardholders facing higher rates, consumer groups recommended contacting the issuer to request a lower rate, considering a lower-cost balance transfer and paying more than the minimum whenever possible. They also cautioned customers to review transfer fees and promotional-rate expiration dates before moving debt.

The controversy added momentum to a broader push in Washington to overhaul credit card rules and protect borrowers from sudden changes at a time of extraordinary financial stress.

The controversy centered on “any time, any reason” repricing. Credit-card issuers could raise a customer’s interest rate even when the customer had paid on time, stayed within the credit limit, and had not otherwise violated the agreement.

Rich Stevens’ experience illustrated the problem: despite maintaining a good payment record, his card issuer sharply increased his rate without identifying misconduct on his part. Because the higher rate could apply to an existing balance, borrowing that had been undertaken at one price suddenly became much more expensive. His choices were essentially to accept the increase or stop using—and potentially close—the account while paying off the balance under the old terms.

Rep. She supported legislation requiring advance notice, limiting retroactive rate increases, and allowing higher rates mainly when there was a legitimate trigger, such as serious delinquency.

Card companies countered that flexible pricing was necessary to manage changing credit risk and funding costs. Critics responded that cases like Stevens’ showed the power was being used arbitrarily, shifting risk to responsible consumers who had done nothing wrong.

counterfactuals.output:
**Citigroup’s Card-Rate Increases Draw Scrutiny After Federal Rescue**

*Bank says repricing reflects higher credit risk, while consumer advocates point to taxpayer support and the banking industry’s influence in Washington.*

**WASHINGTON —** Citigroup’s decision to raise interest rates on some credit-card accounts is intensifying criticism of the banking giant, which received billions of dollars in federal assistance as lawmakers struggled to advance legislation limiting card-industry practices.

The increases came as consumers faced rising unemployment, falling home values and tighter access to credit. Some Citigroup customers received notices that their annual percentage rates would climb sharply unless they rejected the new terms and stopped making new purchases on their cards.

Citigroup has said such pricing decisions reflect worsening economic conditions, higher borrowing costs and the increased likelihood that customers will default. The company has also said affected cardholders generally could opt out, keep their previous rate and repay existing balances, though they would lose the ability to continue using the account.

Consumer advocates argue that the choice offers little protection to families who depend on credit cards for groceries, medical bills and other necessities.

The rate increases drew particular attention because of Citigroup’s reliance on federal support. In 2008, the Treasury Department invested $45 billion in the company through the Troubled Asset Relief Program. The government also agreed to share potential losses on a pool of more than $300 billion in troubled assets, part of an extraordinary effort to stabilize one of the country’s largest financial institutions.

That assistance was intended to protect the broader economy and prevent a disorderly collapse, federal officials said. It did not impose a general prohibition on raising consumer interest rates.

Still, critics say the juxtaposition is stark: Taxpayers helped strengthen Citigroup’s balance sheet while some of those same taxpayers were told to pay more on their credit-card debt.

“Banks are receiving public support on favorable terms, but many customers are not seeing similar relief,” consumer advocates have argued in urging Congress to restrict retroactive and sudden rate increases.

Banking representatives counter that lawmakers risk making credit less available. If lenders cannot adjust rates to account for changing risk, they say, banks may respond by reducing credit limits, increasing upfront rates or closing accounts—particularly those held by borrowers with weaker credit histories.

The dispute has also renewed questions about the financial industry’s political influence. Campaign-finance records show that banks, credit-card companies and other financial firms have long been major sources of federal campaign contributions and lobbying expenditures. Citigroup’s political-action committee and employees have contributed to candidates in both parties. Such donations are legally distinct from taxpayer bailout funds, but watchdog groups say they help the industry maintain access to policymakers.

Banks and their trade associations have lobbied against proposals they consider overly restrictive, while supporting disclosure-based approaches and arguing that federal regulators—not Congress—should set detailed credit-card rules.

In the House, lawmakers approved a “Credit Cardholders’ Bill of Rights” that would have limited certain retroactive rate increases, required more notice before changes and restricted fees and billing practices. The measure stalled in the Senate amid industry opposition, competing legislative priorities and disagreement over how quickly new protections should take effect.

Federal regulators separately adopted credit-card rules intended to curb some practices, including rate increases on existing balances. But those rules were not scheduled to become fully effective until 2010, leaving consumers exposed during the height of the financial crisis, according to supporters of immediate legislation.

The political pressure places lawmakers in a difficult position. They are trying to keep major banks solvent and lending while responding to constituents who say those same institutions are making household debt more expensive.

Citigroup’s rate increases may be legal under existing agreements and regulations. But after a rescue backed by taxpayers, the controversy is no longer only about what card issuers are permitted to do. It is also about what obligations, if any, a federally supported bank owes to the public that helped keep it afloat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
